sources.institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

evidence.estrutura: Steinem’s movement politics emphasize grassroots organizations, networks and social movements rather than centralized executive power; modest decentralist tendency.
evidence.representacao: Women’s political organizing, caucuses and public advocacy strongly support democratic participation and equal representation.
evidence.poder: Reproductive autonomy, opposition to gender violence and civil-rights activism strongly favor personal liberty over coercive moral regulation.
evidence.imigracao: Her intersectional feminism and solidarity politics support multicultural inclusion and opposition to exclusionary identity politics.
evidence.diplomacia: Her activism has generally favored human rights, nonviolence and international feminist solidarity over militarism.
evidence.intervencao: Anti-war and anti-imperialist currents in her activism support restraint and skepticism toward coercive intervention.
evidence.economia: Workplace equality and feminist economic critique support center-left redistribution/regulation rather than either laissez-faire or state ownership.
evidence.controle: Supports regulation and social protections while operating within civil-society liberal politics; moderate control.
evidence.comercio: No distinctive tariff doctrine; internationalist social movements suggest moderate openness with labor/human-rights concerns.
evidence.religiao: Her public feminism is strongly secular and critical of patriarchal religious authority, though not simply anti-religious.
evidence.moral: Reproductive rights, gender equality and LGBTQ-inclusive feminism make her strongly socially progressive.
evidence.tecnologia: Technology is not central; moderately positive toward modern communications and social change.
